title: How often is the queue ten deep?

prereqs.why: The geometric equilibrium distribution of the M/M/1 queue is the result being applied.
The distribution is the stationary one of a continuous-time birth-death chain.
Detailed balance is what turns the stationarity equations into a one-line recursion.

statement:
Customers arrive at a single-server desk as a Poisson process of rate
$\lambda = 8$ per hour, and each service takes an independent
$\mathrm{Exponential}(\mu)$ time with $\mu = 10$ per hour. Customers wait if
the server is busy, and the queue may grow without limit.

Let $X(t)$ be the number of customers present. It is a birth–death chain in
continuous time with birth rate $\lambda$ and death rate $\mu$, so the
detailed balance equations $\pi_i \lambda = \pi_{i+1}\mu$ hold and give

$$\pi_i = (1-\rho)\,\rho^{\,i}, \qquad \rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}, \qquad i \ge 0,$$

which is a distribution precisely when $\rho < 1$.

In equilibrium, find the probability that there are **at least ten**
customers present.

Give the answer as a decimal to **three decimal places**; it is checked to
within $\pm 0.001$.
hints: Work out $\rho$ first. It is the long-run fraction of time the server is busy.
$\P(X \ge 10) = \sum_{i \ge 10} (1-\rho)\rho^{\,i}$, which is a geometric series starting at $i = 10$.
That series collapses: the factor $(1-\rho)$ cancels against the sum of the series and a single power of $\rho$ is left.

payload.prompt: The equilibrium probability of ten or more customers present.
payload.label: $\P(X \ge 10) \approx$
payload.syntax: A decimal, to three decimal places. Checked to within 0.001.
